clips.title: AWS EC2 Auto Scaling - How it Works
clips.why: A clear diagram of an Auto Scaling group and its settings, the base that warm pools are added to.
look: Minimum, maximum and desired capacity: our groups use 0, 3 and 0.
The group launches VMs from a launch template, so every VM gets the same rules.
clips.after: Our groups keep nothing running: desired is 0 until a run asks, and the warm pool next to the group holds the ready VMs.

clips.title: EC2 Auto Scaling Warm Pools | Warm Pools | EC2 Auto Scaling
clips.why: Why slow-starting machines are a problem for scaling, and how a warm pool of prepared machines solves it.
look: The problem first: a new VM that needs a long setup before it is useful.
The warm pool as prepared VMs kept outside the desired capacity.
The pool states, and why a stopped pool is the cheap one.
clips.after: A sandbox's long setup is pulling the product's images and starting it once, which is exactly what our pool does before the VM goes to sleep.

clips.title: Auto Scaling | Lifecycle Hooks Made Easier
clips.why: A one-minute official explanation of lifecycle hooks: a pause in a VM's launch for your own setup.
look: The VM waits in a pending state until the hook is completed.
Your own code decides when setup is done.
clips.after: Our hook waits up to 30 minutes for the image's setup service to warm the VM and call CompleteLifecycleAction.

clips.title: Amazon/AWS EC2 Pricing Simply Explained | On-Demand, Spot, Reserved, Savings Plans
clips.why: Creating a Spot instance step by step, with the price difference and the interruption behaviour in view.
look: How much cheaper the Spot price is than the on-demand price for the same type.
What happens to the VM when AWS needs the capacity back.
clips.after: The CI fixer and the other routines take that deal because they checkpoint after every step; Nova does not, because it waits on people.

practice.q: Complete the warm pool setting that makes sure a VM which served a run is destroyed instead of going back to the pool.
practice.hint: The CLI skeleton's default is the opposite.
practice.why: A used VM may hold anything a fooled run left on it, so one fresh VM per run means it never returns to the pool.

practice.q: Put the life of a warm-pool VM in order, from launch to its run.
items: The group launches a new VM from the full launch template
The setup service reads Warmed:Stopped from the metadata service
It starts the product once to pull the images, then stops it
It calls CompleteLifecycleAction, and AWS stops the VM in the pool
A run raises the desired capacity, and the VM starts in about a minute
The run detaches the VM, and the pool prepares a replacement
practice.why: All the slow, identical work happens before the VM sleeps, so the only wait a run sees is the start of a stopped machine.

practice.q: The metadata path spot/instance-action answers 404. What does that mean?

options.text: The VM is not a Spot VM
options.why: A Spot VM also answers 404 there, as long as AWS has not decided to take it back.

options.text: There is no interruption notice yet, so keep working and ask again
options.why: The path only exists after AWS posts the notice. That is why spot-watch must treat 404 as "no notice".

options.text: The metadata service is turned off
options.why: Other paths still answer. 404 means only that this one item does not exist yet.

practice.q: The warm pool is empty when a run asks for a full VM. What happens?

options.text: The run fails with an error
options.why: The group still launches a VM. It is a cold start, not a failure.

options.text: The group launches a new VM from scratch, which takes longer, and the orchestrator counts it as a cold start
options.why: Raising the desired capacity always gives a VM; only the speed changes. Counting cold starts shows when the pool is too small.

options.text: The run takes a VM that just finished another run
options.why: Used VMs are never reused. One fresh VM per run is a wall.

practice.q: A teammate's watcher reads the notice with plain curl -s, and the routine exits almost at once every time. Complete the curl option that fixes it.
practice.hint: The option that makes curl fail on an HTTP error such as 404.
practice.why: A 404 still sends an HTML page. Without -f, curl succeeds, the page looks like a notice, and the routine thinks it is being interrupted.
